newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.

text.p: BEAZLEY: GOVT MUST SEND MESSAGE TO CAR INDUSTRY
Opposition leader, Kim Beazley, says the Government has to let companies that invest in the car industry know Australia is serious about keeping them here, and about aiding their export drives.
Mr Beazley's comments come as pressure builds on the Government to freeze car industry tariffs, ahead of the release of a report by the Productivity Commission into the subject.

The commission's draft report proposed slashing car tariffs from the current rate of 22.5 per cent to five per cent by 2004. The Opposition and industry groups want tariffs to be frozen at 15 per cent until 2005.
The Government's expected to announce its final position within two weeks.
VANSTONE SAYS MAY HAVE INADVERTENTLY MISLED THE SENATE
Federal Employment minister Amanda Vanstone has told a Senate Committee hearing there's a distinct possibility she inadvertently misled the Senate last week.
The Opposition claims Senator Vanstone misled the Senate when she said it was against the state law to charge a jobseeker for employment payment services.
The Opposition says in her home state of South Australia the law says a jobseeker can be charged a deposit and the deposit can be applied towards a fee.
Senator Vanstone now says the Government remains convinced there will no more charging for job searching and job placement than already exists.
EXTORTION ATTEMPT LEADS TO EXTRADITION
A Melbourne man will be extradited to New South Wales to face charges relating to a $4 million extortion bid on the Nestle Food Company.
Thirty-three year old Mark James Milton, of Box Hill, appeared briefly at the Melbourne Magistrate's Court today.
He was arrested overnight and is charged over demands made of the Nestle Company in Sydney.
He'll will be flown to Sydney today and will appear before a New South Wales Magistrate tomorrow.
The Nestle Company allegedly received threats last month in relation to the contamination of food, unless it paid $4 million.
WORKERS BLOW THEIR HORNS AT RESERVE
The Reserve Bank has been given a noisy reminder that the Transport Workers' Union has neither forgotten, nor forgiven, its intervention in a recent wage case.
Around 130 trucks, blowing their horns, drove past the Reserve Bank building in Sydney's Martin Place for two hours this morning.
The protest was timed to coincide with a meeting of the Reserve Bank board.
TWU State Secretary, Steve Hutchins, says the bank cannot undo the harm it has done to union members, but it can learn from its mistakes.
ARMY DEFENDS BLACKHAWK MASS STAND DOWN
The Army says it acted appropriately in grounding all 36 of its Blackhawk helicopters after a minor accident in southern Queensland.
The aircraft were suspended from operations for a fortnight while each was examined.
A fault was found in a bearing in one aircraft's tail rotor.
This part has been replaced in all aircraft.
Army director of Aviation, Colonel Robert Walford, has defended the suspension against claims it was an over-reaction.
Colonel Walford says the proper procedures were followed, bearing in mind the army's currently on a peacetime footing.
WOOLDRIDGE PESSIMISTIC ABOUT HEROIN TRIAL'S CHANCES
Federal Health Minister, Michael Wooldridge, says the Government does not yet have a position on the proposed heroin trial in the ACT.
But Dr Wooldridge says he is pessimistic about the chances of the trial going ahead, saying it cannot proceed without the support of at least Victoria and New South Wales.
The Australian Parliamentary Group for Drug Law Reform has called on the Victorian Government to publicly back the trial, which would prescribe heroin for addicts.
Dr Wooldridge says Victoria is vaguely in favour of the trial, but New South Wales says only that it will not stand in its way.
He says it would be impossible to run trials big enough in stages two and three without the participation of New South Wales.
DOUBT STILL SURROUNDS FIREBLIGHT DIAGNOSIS
Extensive tests by world experts have not been able to confirm a New Zealand lab's claim that the plant disease fireblight was found on two plants in the Melbourne Botanic Gardens.
Victoria's Agriculture Minister, Pat McNamara, says tests will continue in a German laboratory.
Victorian fruit growers and plant nurseries are hoping that some areas will be freed from the interstate ban on their produce by the end of this week.
The disease is capable of devastating plants, but does not harm the fruit.
